meta.title: Who really said "It's the Guy You Give Something To That You Can't Please"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Will Rogers did write it — in his syndicated column of 3 January 1926, aimed at a Boston critic. But he introduced it as “the old gag.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It's the Guy You Give Something To That You Can't Please'?
meta.ogDescription: Rogers wrote the line in his 3 January 1926 column, hitting back at a critic with a free seat — then called it “the old gag.” The primary page, verified.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Rogers wrote the sentence, word for word, in his syndicated weekly article of 3 January 1926 — a reply to a Boston music critic who had panned a show the critic got in on a free ticket. The catch is that Rogers introduced it as “the old gag,” so he was passing a saying along rather than claiming to have coined it.

source.heading: The column it comes from

docMeta.dd: Will Rogers Is Prying Into Dictionaries Now
3 January 1926 · syndicated weekly article, McNaught Syndicate — printed in The Lincoln Sunday Star (Nebraska) and the South Bend News-Times (Indiana)
Rogers’s reply to a Boston music critic, “His name is Parker. He writes under the initials H. T. P.,” after the last night of a 75-night tour at Symphony Hall
Rogers’s own words — but he introduced them as “the old gag”

source.excerpt: Got back into Symphony hall in Boston. Can you imagine me appearing at Symphony hall in Boston? From the stock yards at Claremore, Okla., to Symphony hall, Boston! Me, with my repertoire of 150 words (most of them wrong), trying to enlighten the descendants of the Cod. But they were fine. … Just one old boy there that thought we were “desecrating” their temple of art by causing laughter in it. … His name is Parker. He writes under the initials H. T. P. … the other people all paid. Your seat was about the only free one. It’s the old gag; people that pay for things never complain. It’s the guy you give something to that you can’t please.
trail: The wording is Rogers’s own, not a later polish. His syndicated weekly article of 3 January 1926 carries the sentence verbatim: the Library of Congress’s digitized South Bend News-Times of that date ↗ reads “It’s the old gag; people that pay for things never complain. It’s the guy you give something to that you can’t please.”

Quote Investigator reached the same column independently. QI’s investigation ↗ transcribes the passage from the Lincoln Sunday Star printing of 3 January 1926 and then follows the saying forward — a 1963 newspaper piece on a Rogers television special, and a 1973 Oklahoma notice of The Will Rogers Book.

Rogers flagged it as second-hand in the same breath. The words “It’s the old gag” sit immediately in front of the famous sentence, and QI concludes he popularized the statement ↗ rather than originating it — while allowing that he may have meant the situation, not the phrase, was old.

No earlier printing has surfaced. QI’s chronology begins in 1926, and a full-text search of the Library of Congress newspaper corpus for the phrase returns a single hit ↗ — that same 3 January 1926 page. If an older gag exists in print, it has not been found. It is also absent from Wikiquote’s Rogers page ↗ in any section.
source.excerptNote: Ellipses mark cuts within one continuous column. Wording follows the Library of Congress digitized text of the South Bend News-Times printing, cross-checked against Quote Investigator’s transcription of the Lincoln Sunday Star printing; the LOC page’s machine-read text garbles “descendants of the Cod” to “God,” and the reading given here follows Quote Investigator.

source.rightsNote: The line was first published on 3 January 1926 in United States newspapers carrying Rogers’s McNaught Syndicate weekly article. Works published in the United States before 1931 are in the public domain there, which is why the full page can be read freely at the Library of Congress ↗. Note that modern edited collections of Rogers’s writings carry their own editorial copyright; the 1926 newspaper text does not.

author.name: Will Rogers

author.heading: Will Rogers
author.metaLine: 1879–1935 · Cherokee-born humorist, newspaper columnist & film star
author.bio: William Penn Adair Rogers was born on 4 November 1879 in Indian Territory and died on 15 August 1935 in an airplane crash in Alaska Territory. A rope-trick vaudevillian turned national commentator, he wrote for the McNaught Syndicate from 1922 until his death, filing a long weekly article and, from July 1926, a short daily telegram. The Will Rogers Memorial Museum reckons his output at roughly two million words — six books and more than 3,600 newspaper columns — which is exactly why so many unsourced one-liners get pinned on him: he really did say an enormous number of things.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: Nobody is stealing this line from Will Rogers — the primary source is his and it is unambiguous. What travels badly is everything around the line: who invented it, how it is worded, and the joke it was built to land.

items.why: Rogers wrote it, but he did not claim it. His own sentence begins “It’s the old gag,” and Quote Investigator concludes that he popularized the statement rather than invented it ↗ — while noting the phrasing is ambiguous as to whether the saying was old or merely the situation.

items.who: “It’s the guy that you give something to”
items.why: A 1963 newspaper television write-up printed the line with an extra “that,” and that variant is still in circulation; a 1973 Oklahoma notice of The Will Rogers Book printed it without. Both printings are transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. The 1926 original has no “that.”

items.who: The line as a standalone aphorism
items.why: Quote pages almost always drop the first half — “people that pay for things never complain” — and always drop the line that makes it a joke rather than a maxim: “Your seat was about the only free one.” It is a wisecrack aimed at one named critic, visible in the digitized 1926 page ↗, not a general observation about human nature.

misattribution.truthLine: Rogers wrote it and made it famous; he told you himself it was already old. The safe form of the credit is “Will Rogers, syndicated column, 3 January 1926” — which is exactly where the documented trail begins ↗.

context.heading: A free seat, a bad review, and a very old gag
lead: Rogers had been on the road 75 nights when he finished the tour at Symphony Hall in Boston — a booking he found hilarious on its face. “From the stock yards at Claremore, Okla., to Symphony hall, Boston!” he wrote. “Me, with my repertoire of 150 words (most of them wrong), trying to enlighten the descendants of the Cod.” By his account the whole tour had passed without a single adverse notice.

Then one reviewer broke the streak. Rogers names him in the column — “His name is Parker. He writes under the initials H. T. P.” — and takes the customary revenge of the performer: he points out that the critic was the only person in the building who had not bought a ticket. That is the setup the famous line resolves, and almost nobody who repeats the line has ever seen it.
context.detailsSummary: What the critic actually objected to
detailsBody: Rogers summarises the complaint as an objection to laughter in a concert hall: “Just one old boy there that thought we were ‘desecrating’ their temple of art by causing laughter in it.” He then runs through the specifics with visible enjoyment — the reviewer was “sore at our quartette because there was only four of them in it,” the Coolidge jokes were “Off Key,” the diction was poor, the selections extremely bad.
He concedes exactly one point. Having done a stretch of football material, he allows: “I should have known better than to talk football near Harvard, where they don’t know anything about it.”
context.pull: Your seat was about the only free one.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator dates the earliest appearance to Will Rogers's syndicated column of 3 January 1926 in The Lincoln Sunday Star, transcribes "It's the old gag; people that pay for things never complain. It's the guy you give something to that you can't please," records that Rogers labelled it an "old gag," concludes he popularized rather than originated it, and lists later printings in 1963 (The Morning Herald, Hagerstown MD) and 1973 (Stilwell Democrat-Journal, on The Will Rogers Book). The 1963 printing reads "the guy that you give something to."

The Library of Congress's machine-read text for this digitized page — South Bend News-Times, South Bend, Indiana, 3 January 1926, Part One, image 6 — literally contains "Your seat was about the only free one. It's the old gag; people that pay for things never complain. It's the guy you give something to that you can't please," together with the Symphony Hall Boston passage, the "desecrating their temple of art" line, the critic "His name is Parker. He writes under the initials H. T. P.", and the column heading "Will Rogers Is Prying Into All the Dictionaries Now!" Verified via the Library of Congress word-coordinates text service for this page's ALTO segment, which returned the snippets verbatim.

A full-text search of the Library of Congress Chronicling America collection for the phrase "guy you give something to" returns exactly one result: South Bend News-Times, 3 January 1926, image 6. No earlier printing appears in that corpus. Verified against the same query's JSON response, which reported a total of 1.

Will Rogers was born 4 November 1879 near Oologah, Indian Territory, and died 15 August 1935 in Alaska Territory in an airplane crash, aged 55; he wrote for the McNaught Syndicate between 1922 and 1935, with a weekly column syndicated from 1922 and a short daily column beginning in 1926.

The Wikiquote page for Will Rogers does NOT contain "It's the guy you give something to that you can't please" or "People that pay for things never complain" in any section. The page does carry sections for Weekly columns, Daily telegrams, several book sources, and a Misattributed section.

The Will Rogers Memorial Museum states that Rogers published approximately two million words in print — six books, over 3,600 newspaper columns, and numerous magazine articles — between his first newspaper article in 1916 and his last in August 1935, and that his Daily Telegrams ran from July 1926 until his death in August 1935.
